category_feedback.specific_evidence: expanded_walkthrough names a real, concrete Grade-3 trap ('empty-lane confusion' — child fills R1 fully but leaves R2 partially blank) with concrete recovery moves (WAIT cards, full templates, drill 'every cell has an action'). However, the trap is not anchored in named CT/computational-thinking research, and recovery_moves do not branch by what the diagnostic told you about the child — the three moves apply identically to every learner.
category_feedback.required_fix: Anchor the trap in named CT research (e.g., Bers 2019 ScratchJr coding misconceptions; Grover & Pea 2013 computational thinking K-3; or Selby & Woollard 2014 on parallelism). Branch recovery: if child can name what R2 should do but forgot to write it, hand a WAIT card and drill 'every cell, every step'; if child cannot conceive that R2 must have ANY action when R1 is acting, drop back to a 2-body physical demo where two children stand side-by-side and one MUST stay still on each spoken count.

category_feedback.specific_evidence: Materials are teacher-makeable (chart paper, index cards, robot markers can be bottle caps), the puppet is explicitly OPTIONAL with substitutes ('teacher voices both characters in two distinct voices, or substitutes two stuffed animals / paper-bag puppets'), and 12/25/13=50 min is realistic for Grade 3. However, the lesson does NOT offer a fully fleshed no-paper, no-purchase fallback. differentiation.for_movement_learners only says 'Act out as 2 robots' — too terse to count as the no-materials alternative path the Level 4 descriptor requires.
category_feedback.required_fix: Expand the no-materials option in differentiation: 'No-materials version — use floor tape or two parallel rows of desks as the 2 lanes. Two children become R1 and R2; they step forward / turn / freeze (WAIT) on each spoken time-step. Loops are chanted: "Repeat 3: forward, forward, forward." Their bodies are the code — no grid mat, no cards, no markers needed.' Add it as a labelled 'No-materials version' inside differentiation so any teacher running the lesson without prep can use it.

category_feedback.specific_evidence: Buzz anchors minds_on, action ('Buzz says — concurrent code can have loops in either lane'), and consolidation ('Buzz's Writing Brag'). All success_criteria start with 'I can'. Vocabulary has child-friendly definitions in blueprint. However, Buzz lacks a distinctive quotable refrain that children chant back, and the exit_routine is a fill-in sentence frame ('R1: ___. R2: ___. They both end at ___.') — useful, but not a memorable chant tied to the character that children carry to Lessons 3-5.
category_feedback.required_fix: Give Buzz a signature refrain children chant back, e.g., 'BUZZ says: every LANE, every STEP, gets an ACTION!' or 'Same step? Same time! That's CONCURRENT!' Embed it in the teacher_script ('Class chants: "every lane, every step, gets an action!"') and add it to the consolidation/exit_routine so Lessons 3-5 can reuse it. The chant should be 6-10 words, rhythmic, and tied to the empty-lane rule.

category_feedback.specific_evidence: Worksheet Parts 1, 2, 3 each map to a named success criterion (4 time-steps synchronised; includes a loop; predicts ending positions), and image_assets list 2-lane templates that mirror the lesson's grid mat. However, the worksheet is largely a rote repeat of the three station tasks; it does NOT deliberately vary the practice format as a transfer task, and teacher_notes does not justify any variation. Part 3 says 'Write your own 2-lane code... predict positions' — same task as the lesson.
category_feedback.required_fix: In Part 3, vary the format to verify transfer/generalization: e.g., 'Both robots must END on the same square. Write a 2-lane code (4-6 steps) that makes this happen — at least one lane uses a loop.' This reverses the task (target outcome, design code) instead of free-writing. Add a teacher_notes line: 'Part 3 is a transfer task — children reverse-engineer code from a desired outcome, verifying they understand WHY each step matters, not just that they can write any 2-lane code.'

category_feedback.specific_evidence: Conceptual progression is explicit: time-step model is taught precisely ('Each row is one moment. Both lanes' actions happen in that moment'), WAIT is introduced as a real action, vocabulary (concurrent, sequential, repeating) is used precisely, and the grid mat carries time-step meaning. However, expanded_walkthrough.rationale does NOT name the misconception in research-grounded CT terms (e.g., Bers 2019, Grover & Pea 2013, Selby & Woollard 2014 on parallelism), and children do not compare/refine each other's strategies — the stretch is individual, not comparative.
category_feedback.required_fix: In expanded_walkthrough.rationale, name the trap as 'parallelism-as-sequence conflation / empty-lane error (Bers 2019 ScratchJr; Grover & Pea 2013, computational thinking K-3; Selby & Woollard 2014 on parallel events).' Add a consolidation move where two pairs swap codes and explain: 'Whose robots finish at the same time? Whose finish at different times? Why?' — children compare and refine each other's strategies, anchoring the time-step model.

summary: Pair 2 is achieving-level work with strong alignment (Lesson 2 explicitly bridges from Lesson 1: 'Yesterday we IDENTIFIED concurrent. Today we WRITE...') and a real Grade-3 trap (empty-lane confusion). However, five of six categories sit at Level 3. The lesson needs a named CT research anchor, branched recovery moves, an expanded no-materials fallback, a quotable Buzz chant, and a strategy-comparison move; the worksheet needs Part 3 reframed as a transfer task with a justified outcome-target. With five 3s, the strict pair bar (max one 3) is not met — revise both lesson_02 and worksheet_02.
